methods: using sin x cos x = (1/2) sin 2x
statement: By using the substitution $x=\\pi/2-t$ and the identity $\\sin x\\cos x=\\tfrac12\\sin2x$, show that $\\int_{0}^{\\pi/2}\\ln(\\sin x)\,dx=-\\frac{\\pi}{2}\\ln2$.
solution: Let $I=\\int_{0}^{\\pi/2}\\ln(\\sin x)\,dx$. The substitution $x=\\pi/2-t$ gives $I=\\int_{0}^{\\pi/2}\\ln(\\cos t)\,dt$. Adding, $2I=\\int_{0}^{\\pi/2}\\ln(\\sin x\\cos x)\,dx=\\int_{0}^{\\pi/2}\\ln\\bigl(\\tfrac12\\sin2x\bigr)\,dx=\\int_{0}^{\\pi/2}\\ln(\\sin2x)\,dx-\\int_{0}^{\\pi/2}\\ln2\,dx$. With $u=2x$, $\\int_{0}^{\\pi/2}\\ln(\\sin2x)\,dx=\\tfrac12\\int_{0}^{\\pi}\\ln(\\sin u)\,du=\\tfrac12\\cdot2I=I$ by symmetry. Thus $2I=I-\\frac{\\pi}{2}\\ln2$, so $I=-\\frac{\\pi}{2}\\ln2$.
hints: Show the integral of ln sin equals that of ln cos.
Combine the logs into ln((1/2) sin2x).
Rescale the sin2x integral back to I using symmetry.
